newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Mexico's Bimbo may have $2 bln '97 sales.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mexico's Bimbo may have $2 bln '97 sales.

text.p: Grupo Industrial Bimbo SA, Mexico's bread, cakes and cookies giant, expects 1997 sales to be "perhaps" around $2 billion, Corporate President Rafael Velez Valadez told Reuters in an interview.
Sales in 1996 rose to 15.102 billion pesos, up from 12.974 billion in 1995, according to Bimbo's 1996 annual statement.
Velez Valadez said the company expects sales volume to grow four percent this year. He said the second quarter was going "reasonably well."
"Sales have been sustained (compared to the first quarter)" he added. He also classified the first quarter as a "reasonable" quarter.

Bimbo plans to invest $180 million this year, around 80 percent of which will go into the company's Mexican operations, Velez Valadez said. In late May, Bimbo opened a plant producing bread, cakes and tortillas, Mexico's corn flour pancakes, in the southeastern city of Merida. Other projects in Mexico include a wheat milling plant in the northern city of Monterrey to be started up in September and a new corn mill in the central state of Hidalgo at Tula.
Velez Valadez said these projects, coupled with fleet renovations, would be the majority of the national investments this year.

Bimbo runs a distribution network with 14,000 vehicles making deliveries to 400,000 sales points. The average vehicle life is 10 years. "That means we have to buy more than 1,000 new vehicles each year," he said, indicating another sizeable part of the planned investment for 1997.
Velez Valadez said Bimbo had boosted payroll numbers this year in what he called "general job growth." To May, he said, the company employed 53,350 versus 49,000 at the end of 1996.
On Bimbo's international operations, Velez Valadez said the company intended to consolidate operations for the next two years after several years of rapid growth and expansions.

In Latin America, Bimbo expanded rapidly in the early 1990s and now has plants in Argentina, Chile, Venezuela, Colombia, Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica and distribution centers in Honduras and Nicaragua.
"The plan is to consolidate...I believe these plants will be consolidated in two years at the latest," he said.
On further expansions in Latin America, he said both Brazil and Peru were under study. "But there is nothing concrete," he stressed.
